items.source_name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
items.title: Cumulative thermal stress predicts functional change in coral reef fish communities
items.author: Anthony C. Markey et al.
items.raw_text: Marine heatwaves are altering coral reef fish communities through a combination of direct impacts of thermal stress and indirect impacts that degrade coral habitats. Impacts may vary for species in different functional groups (e.g. herbivore replacement of corallivores), altering the functional composition of fish communities that is critical to reef resilience. However, our understanding of trait-based responses of fish communities to marine heatwaves is inadequate, and mostly inferred from local scales and low numbers of species. Here, we use a Bayesian joint species distribution model based on data for 500 fish species from 286 sites surveyed across northern Australia to evaluate the impacts of marine heatwaves on species probability of occurrence and their interactions with four functional traits. The effects of degree heating weeks and coral loss on individual species probability of occurrence had the highest total and proportionally negative responses, respectively. Thermal affinity's positive response to cumulative heat stress (i.e. degree heating weeks) was the strongest trait effect. Community-level analyses predicted losses in habitat specialists, large-bodied fishes, corallivores and pelagic feeders along a gradient of marine heatwave stress. The loss and restructuring of functional diversity suggest that heatwaves will continue eroding fish-dependent ecological roles and associated ecosystem services.

extra.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
extra.gist: Marine heatwaves shift coral reef fish communities toward herbivores at the expense of corallivores, altering functional composition that reef resilience depends on. A Bayesian model across multiple species and locations provides predictive insight into how thermal stress reorganizes fish communities.

items.title: Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
items.author: Alexia Karwat et al.
items.raw_text: Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

extra.gist: Marine heatwave frequency and intensity in coral reef regions are predictable on multi-year timescales using Earth system models, with skill varying by region. Extended forecasting could enable proactive reef management and conservation planning.

items.title: Why might corals settle on Lithophyllum prototypum? A hypothesis linking non-geniculate coralline algal architecture to coral recruitment
items.author: Renato C. Pereira
items.raw_text: Coral recruitment depends on the ability of larvae to identify suitable benthic substrates, and non-geniculate coralline algae are among the most important natural facilitators of this process. Within this group, members of the Lithophyllum prototypum complex are repeatedly associated with high coral settlement responses, but the mechanisms underlying this effect remain incompletely understood. Most explanations have emphasized chemical and microbial cues, whereas the distinctive surface architecture of this morphotype has received little ecological attention. Here, we characterize the applanate surface architecture of the Lithophyllum prototypum complex using scanning electron microscopy and quantitative morphometry. Repeated thallus superimposition generates applanate branches, characterized by overlapping lamellae, elevated margins, narrow crevices and interstitial spaces distributed across the algal surface. The mean spacing between adjacent applanate branches was 533 ± 213 µm, while overhanging lamellar margins formed shallow cavities averaging 29.1 ± 5.6 µm in height. These dimensions suggest that the surface of this morphotype produces larval-scale microhabitats rather than deep cryptic shelters. We hypothesize that this architecture may enhance coral settlement by increasing contact opportunities, promoting larval retention and modulating the local expression of chemical and microbial cues. This physical–chemical–microbial microhabitat hypothesis provides a testable framework for re-evaluating how NGCA morphology contributes to coral recruitment.

extra.gist: Non-geniculate coralline algae in the Lithophyllum prototypum complex consistently trigger high coral larval settlement, but the mechanism remains unclear. Surface architecture may play an underappreciated role alongside chemical and microbial settlement cues.

items.title: Decoding the metagenome of the precious red coral: discovery of a new spirochete lineage and carotenoid-producing bacteria
items.author: R. Tignat-Perrier et al.
items.raw_text: Abstract The precious red coral Corallium rubrum is an ecologically and economically iconic Mediterranean octocoral, yet the diversity and functions of its microbiome remain a “blackbox” at the genomic scale. Here, we present a genome-resolved metagenomic analysis of C. rubrum , reconstructing 25 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), including 16 from wild colonies and 9 additional ones from a laboratory colony, to gain insight into the functional potential of its microbiome. Our phylogenomic analysis of the two dominant Spirochaetota symbionts reveals that one of the two symbionts represents a potential novel, previously undescribed lineage, which appears to be exclusively associated with octocoral species. Functional profiling indicates that these Spirochaetota exhibit different metabolic pathways, and are adapted to the symbiotic life, probably representing mutualistic partners for C. rubrum . Their genomes encode biosynthetic pathways of a wide range of essential amino acids and vitamins, and the capacity to ferment sugars to acetate, potentially supplementing host dietary deficiencies. We also identified an interesting symbiont, affiliated with the Qipengyuania genus, that possesses the genomic potential for the biosynthesis of the carotenoid canthaxanthin, one of the main pigments involved in the red color of C. rubrum . The other MAGs encode a wide range of metabolic pathways, especially those linked to nitrogen and sulfur transformations. Our findings suggest potential metabolic interactions between the red coral host and its microbiome. This study offers detailed taxonomic and functional characterization of newly identified octocoral symbionts, establishing a foundation for future investigations into octocoral symbiotic relationships.

extra.gist: Metagenomic analysis of precious red coral reveals 25 bacterial genomes including a new spirochete lineage and carotenoid-producing symbionts. Understanding coral microbiota function deepens knowledge of what keeps corals alive.

items.title: Implications of hardbottom sponge community decline for ecosystem function in the Florida Keys, Florida (USA)
items.author: Mark J. Butler
items.raw_text: Human damage to the marine ecosystem of the Florida Keys may have begun in pre-Columbian times but expanded with European colonization about 400 years ago, particularly through overfishing of large species such as seals, turtles, and groupers. Around the turn of the 20th century, draining of the Everglades and construction of the overseas railway altered forever the flow of fresh and saltwater in the ecosystem. But by and large, the resilience of the ecosystem remained intact until the late 1970’s-early 1980’s when it began to collapse, exemplified by phytoplankton blooms, seagrass and sponge die-offs, mass urchin mortalities, and coral disease. Today, seagrass meadows are relatively healthy but coral reefs harbor few corals and inshore hardbottom habitats have been stripped of sponges and octocorals among other taxa. Changes to hardbottom sponge communities between 2002 and 2018 throughout the Florida Keys are documented here, as are the ramifications of sponge loss on local benthic scouring, underwater soundscapes, and the effect on waterborne microbial communities and water chemistry by sponge filtration. From 2002-2018, sponge abundance and diversity declined by 66% and 34% (respectively), even in regions that did not experience sponge-killing cyanobacteria blooms. Without the presence of large sponges, benthic scouring is reduced, which promotes sedimentation and may hasten the transition of hardbottom habitat to seagrass. Loud, acoustically complex hardbottom soundscapes become acoustic dead-zones without soniferous species associated with large sponges, dampening the sonic signatures that larvae and other animal life stages use to navigate to hardbottom. The decline in sponges and the effects of their lost filtration is estimated to have reduced ecosystem-level removal of DOC by 30 – 56% and NH4 by 40% along with an approximate 30% reduction in the release by sponges into the water of PO4 and NO2-NO3. extra.gist: Florida Keys hardbottom sponge communities have declined, threatening reef ecosystem function. Understanding reef-system collapse informs conservation priorities and baseline knowledge for coral-reef biology.

items.title: Culture and Isolation of Bacteria Associated with Mediterranean Corals
items.author: Rocio Mozo et al.
items.raw_text: Abstract Corals harbor a diverse bacterial community that facilitates adaptation and sustains their health. In coral holobiont research, culture-independent approaches have transformed the existing paradigm. Molecular techniques, such as metabarcoding, revealed a high diversity of previously unrecognized bacterial symbionts. Coral microbiota characterization has relied on these techniques over the last decade, but relying solely on them does not provide a detailed understanding of the dynamics of the coral holobiont complex. Returning to classic microbiological methods and in vitro experimentation can yield novel insights into symbiont roles, physiology, and interactions within the holobiont. Under this premise, we aimed to isolate and culture bacteria from four Mediterranean coral species: Eunicella singularis , Cladocora caespitosa , Leptogorgia sarmentosa , and Paramuricea clavata . The recovery of 84 pure bacterial isolates and their initial classification based on the 16S rRNA gene revealed a diverse community of culturable coral-associated bacteria spanning four classes and 20 genera. Among these, six isolates may represent novel taxa (< 97% 16S rRNA identity to their closest described species) within Vibrio , Pseudoalteromonas , Alteromonas , Shewanella and Tritonibacter , underscoring the value of culture-based studies. The cultured bacterial diversity included taxa exhibiting traits potentially involved in host association, biofilm formation, surface colonization, and degradation of complex polysaccharides, suggesting functional roles in coral colonization and holobiont maintenance. Establishing this bacterial culture collection provides a foundation for investigating bacterial roles within the coral holobiont through detailed morphological and physiological characterization and experimental ecology studies.

extra.gist: A review argues culturable bacterial methods are essential alongside molecular techniques to understand coral holobiont dynamics. Classical microbiology reveals coral symbiont behavior that sequencing alone cannot.

items.source_name: Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries
items.title: Quantifying surgeonfish functions in coral reef sediment dynamics: an ecological and evolutionary perspective
items.author: Isabelle Ng et al.
items.raw_text: Fish-driven ecosystem functions directly contribute to sediment dynamics on coral reefs, shaping how reefs operate in the present-day and potentially through evolutionary time. However, our understanding of these biologically-mediated sediment processes and their underlying evolutionary history remains poorly resolved for surgeonfishes (Acanthuridae), despite their known role in reef sediment dynamics. To fill this knowledge gap, we combined detailed field sampling and phylogenetic comparative methods to quantify the functional role of surgeonfishes in the past and present. Phylogenetic generalised linear mixed models revealed a positive association between body size and the mass of sediment ingested across all surgeonfish functional groups. At an assemblage-level and individual body-mass-standardised scale, brushers and sediment suckers – united by their possession of gizzard-like stomachs – ingested the most sediment relative to other functional groups. However, the larger overall body size of sediment-sucking surgeonfishes means that they ingest the highest sediment masses, individually and relative to all other functional groups across reef habitats at Lizard Island. Surprisingly, grain-size composition did not differ substantially between the gizzard-like stomachs and the intestines of brushers and sediment suckers, suggesting that grain-size modification is not a major function performed by surgeonfishes. Finally, we detected a shift towards greater sediment ingestion in the Miocene (~15–17 million years ago) that temporally aligns with the evolution of gizzard-like stomachs in detritivorous surgeonfishes (i.e. sediment suckers and brushers) and the early formation of modern reefs. These findings showcase the extent to which surgeonfishes may have been, and continue to be, key contributors to reef sediment dynamics.

extra.venue: Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries
extra.gist: Phylogenetic study quantifying surgeonfish roles in coral reef sediment dynamics across evolutionary time. Advances understanding of how a key reef-fish family shapes reef structure and function.

items.title: Generating blue carbon credits through conservation of Posidonia oceanica: experience from the LIFE SeaForest project
items.author: Marco Marcelli
items.raw_text: IntroductionPosidonia oceanica meadows are key blue carbon ecosystems in the Mediterranean Sea, storing substantial carbon within biomass and underlying sediments. Unregulated recreational anchoring contributes to meadow degradation and may compromise the retention of previously stored carbon. The LIFE SeaForest project (LIFE17 CCM/IT/000121) aimed to reduce carbon losses associated with P. oceanica degradation through integrated management, monitoring, conservation, and restoration actions across three Mediterranean protected coastal areas.MethodsA comprehensive ex-ante accounting framework was developed to estimate anchoring-related potential carbon-stock losses, expressed in CO2-equivalent units, under baseline (business-as-usual) and project scenarios. The methodology considered vessel-size classes and substrate categories associated with P. oceanica (rocky, sandy, and degraded dead matte substrates). Project actions included environmentally friendly mooring systems, sustainable anchoring management plans, and regulation of recreational boating through a dedicated digital user platform.ResultsOver the ten-year accounting period, cumulative Net Emission Reductions (NERs) exceeded 5,000 tCO2eq across the three project areas. This value represents net avoided potential carbon-stock loss, rather than directly quantified atmospheric CO2 emissions, and identifies a potential SeaForest credit volume subject to monitoring, verification, and certification.DiscussionThe proposed framework represents one of the first structured ex-ante approaches for estimating potential blue carbon credits from conservation measures that reduce anchoring impacts in Mediterranean P. oceanica meadows. Although further validation and long-term monitoring are needed, the SeaForest approach provides a potentially replicable framework for blue carbon initiatives, sustainable coastal management, and climate-mitigation policies in the Mediterranean region.

extra.gist: LIFE SeaForest project develops accounting frameworks for blue-carbon credits through Posidonia oceanica conservation in the Mediterranean. Seagrass meadow carbon storage and degradation dynamics inform reef-adjacent ecosystem management and conservation valuation.

items.source_name: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
items.title: Microbial Community Structure and Predicted Functional Potential Across Environmental Gradients Influenced by Submarine Groundwater Discharge in Tropical Coral Reef Intertidal Sediments
items.author: Feng‐Yu Wang et al.
items.raw_text: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) delivers land-derived nutrients to coastal waters, but its effects on benthic microbial communities in tropical coral reef intertidal sediments are largely unknown. We studied the Duzaiping Marine Protected Area on Liuqiu Island, Taiwan, where groundwater seeps through a coral reef limestone platform. Surface sediments and bottom water from 19 sites were analyzed for dissolved nutrients, 16S rRNA amplicon diversity, and predicted functional potential (FAPROTAX). Groundwater discharge points had salinities of 2–3 and NO2− + NO3−, PO43−, and SiO2 concentrations up to 623.94, 7.07, and 245.83 µM, respectively. Principal component analysis resolved three geochemically distinct groups: Groundwater (GW), Mixed, and Seawater (SW). Microbial communities were significantly differentiated between GW and SW groups. Nitrospiraceae, Nitrosomonadaceae, Burkholderiaceae, and Pseudomonadaceae were enriched at the discharge points, consistent with nitrification and putative denitrification. Halieaceae and Xenococcaceae were most abundant in the marine-dominated zone. Predicted aerobic ammonia and nitrite oxidation were enriched in GW sediments, whereas predicted fermentation was enriched in SW sediments. Woeseiaceae abundance correlated positively with phosphate and predicted nitrification. SGD thus alters nutrient stoichiometry and sorts benthic microbial communities, with predicted functional profiles shifting from nitrogen transformation near discharge points to heterotrophic decomposition in marine-dominated sediments.

extra.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
extra.gist: Submarine groundwater discharge through coral reef sediments introduces nutrient gradients that reshape benthic microbial communities and their metabolic function. Understanding these geochemical influences on reef microbiota is relevant to nutrient cycling in reef systems.

items.title: Density patterns and age structure of the queen conch ( Aliger gigas ) in a coral reef lagoon in the Mexican Caribbean
items.author: Isvi Areli Benítez-Castillo et al.
items.raw_text: The queen conch ( Aliger gigas ) is one of the most important fishery resources in the Caribbean; however, its populations have declined markedly as a result of overexploitation. This study evaluated the population density and size structure of the species within the Banco Chinchorro Biosphere Reserve, Mexico, during 2015, 2016, and 2018, encompassing the final phase of a 5-year total fishing closure and the period immediately following its termination. A total of 35 sampling stations were distributed across six zones of the reef lagoon. At each station, five circular surveys with an 8 m radius were conducted during each sampling campaign. The highest densities were observed in the Central and Southern Leeward zones, whereas the lowest occurred in the Southern Windward zone. Population density increased during the fishing closure and reached its maximum in 2016, suggesting a partial recovery associated with reduced fishing pressure. Despite this increase, the population was dominated by juveniles and subadults, while sexually mature individuals represented only a small proportion of the stock. Spatial variation in size distribution revealed distinct areas functioning as recruitment, growth, and potentially reproductive habitats within the reserve. Conversely, the scarcity of large individuals suggests the long-term effects of selective harvesting on the adult component of the population. Comparison between siphonal length and lip thickness indicated that only 6.2% of individuals simultaneously met the legal minimum harvest size and a morphological criterion associated with sexual maturity, whereas 10.03% attained the minimum legal size without having reached reproductive maturity. These findings indicate that siphonal length alone may not adequately protect the reproductive stock of A. gigas . Accordingly, size-based management regulations should be complemented by biological indicators of maturity, such as lip thickness, to enhance conservation measures and promote

extra.gist: Queen conch populations in a Mexican Caribbean lagoon show recovery during and after a 5-year fishing closure, with density and age structure tracked across reefs. Population response to protection measures informs management of this overexploited Caribbean resource.

items.title: Contribución de la ictiofauna arrecifal a los servicios ecosistémicos del Sistema Arrecifal Mesoamericano
items.author: Bárbara Velázquez-Rivera et al.
items.raw_text: Introduction: Ecosystem services (ES) are benefits derived from ecological processes that contribute to human well-being. Coral reefs and their fish communities provide multiple ES, but they face growing threats in the Mesoamerican Reef System (MRS), where reef degradation affects biodiversity and associated benefits. Although assigning ES at the species level remains a challenge, their assessment is key to conservation and management. Objective: To characterize the contribution of reef fish species included in the Reef Health Index (RHI) to the ES of the Mexican MRS. Materials and Methods: Based on scientific literature, databases, identification guides, and consultations with experts, twelve ecosystem services in the categories of provisioning, regulation, support, and cultural were assigned to 28 species of Epinephelidae, Lutjanidae, and Labridae included in the RHI. Differences in the average number of ES among families and categories were evaluated using ANOVA; hierarchical clustering analyses were performed; and the contribution of fish to ES was calculated using an index at six sites within the Cozumel Reefs National Park (CRNP), relating it to environmental factors and the RHI. Results: All species contributed to multiple ecosystem services, with Epinephelus striatus standing out with seven ecosystem services. Groupers and snappers dominated provisioning services, while parrotfish were primarily responsible for regulatory functions such as herbivory and bioerosion. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences between service categories but not between families. Cluster analyses identified functional groupings related to ecological processes and social benefits. At six sites in the CRNP, the relationships between ecosystem service diversity, environmental variables, and the RHI were weak and not significant. However, the Ecosystem Service Index showed marked spatial heterogeneity, with Chankanaab standing out as the site with the highest value. Concl

extra.gist: A study quantifies how reef fish species in the Mesoamerican Reef contribute to ecosystem services including fisheries, coastal protection, and nutrient cycling. Assigning ecological value species-by-species helps prioritize conservation in a degraded reef system.

items.title: Reassessing carbon sink fisheries: biogeochemical constraints and ecological-economic-social coupling and governance
items.author: Xi Hu
items.raw_text: Fisheries and aquaculture influence marine carbon cycling, but biological carbon-retention does not necessarily constitute atmospheric carbon dioxide removal. This critical narrative review reassesses carbon sink fisheries, a concept developed in Chinese fisheries research, through an ecological-economic-social framework. Seaweed cultivation, bivalve aquaculture, integrated multi-trophic aquaculture, and fisheries management are distinguished by carbon pathways and evidentiary requirements. Calcification, respiration, atmospheric replenishment, counterfactual production, postharvest fate, and storage durability constrain carbon claims. Recent observations support enhanced carbon burial in some depositional farming environments, whereas carbonate chemistry and system-level analyses do not justify classifying conventional bivalve production as verified marine carbon dioxide removal. These findings are reconciled by distinguishing measured transfers and stocks from additional atmospheric removal that persists over a specified horizon. A practical governance sequence is proposed: define the intervention and baseline, evaluate claim-specific evidence, report removal and avoided emissions separately, and assess economic performance alongside enforceable social and ecological safeguards. Shared monitoring, tenure protection, transparent benefit allocation, and a zero-carbon-credit financing scenario make the framework relevant to small producers. System dynamics is retained as a prospective tool for testing feedback and policy trade-offs; no calibrated simulation is presented. Climate claims should follow demonstrated carbon outcomes, while food production, nutrient removal, habitat protection, and livelihoods can justify distinct policy instruments.

extra.gist: Review reassesses carbon-sink fisheries and aquaculture through ecological and carbon-cycling frameworks. Understanding how seaweed and bivalve farming affect marine carbon pathways informs reef conservation and ecosystem dynamics.

items.title: Hypersalinity and environmentally relevant perfluorohexanesulfonic acid independently and interactively impair survival and development in early life stage red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus)
items.author: Kristin Nielsen
items.raw_text: Estuaries serve as critical nursery habitat for many economically and ecologically important marine species, yet they are increasingly subject to salinity extremes driven by drought, reduced freshwater inflow, and coastal urbanization, as well as to contamination by per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) originating in developed watersheds. Despite this convergence of stressors, the effects of PFAS on estuarine fishes remain understudied, particularly in combination with the natural fluctuations that characterize these systems. The present study investigated the interactive effects of osmotic stress and an environmentally informed concentration of an understudied replacement PFAS, perfluorohexanesulfonic acid (PFHxS), on early life stage (ELS) red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus). Embryos from four independent spawns were exposed to 0 or 1 µg/L PFHxS at four salinities (30, 35, 39 and 43 ppt) in a fully crossed factorial design, using dish as the experimental unit (96 dishes; 1, 920 embryos). PFHxS reduced the odds of hatching by approximately 60%, which carried through to an approximately 36% reduction in the odds of cumulative survival to 48 h that was most pronounced at intermediate salinities. PFHxS did not affect post-hatch survival of larvae that successfully hatched, whereas hypersalinity independently reduced both hatching and post-hatch survival. Among surviving larvae, PFHxS reduced relative yolk sac area and relative brain area and increased the odds of unpigmented eyes approximately five-fold. Results reported herein demonstrate that an environmentally informed concentration of PFHxS is sufficient to adversely affect both the survival and the development of an estuarine-dependent sportfish and address several important data gaps pertaining to the biological risks of replacement PFAS, including multi-stressor interactions and effects on the early development of a large-bodied marine species.

extra.gist: Hypersalinity and perfluorohexanesulfonic acid (a PFAS contaminant) individually and together impair survival and development in red drum larvae. Estuarine fish nurseries face converging stressors from drought and industrial contamination that interact unpredictably.

items.source_name: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
items.title: Observed Spectral-Reflectance Zoning for Model Selection in Satellite-Derived Bathymetry of Heterogeneous Coral Reef Waters Using ICESat-2 and Sentinel-2
items.author: Yuan Le et al.
items.raw_text: Accurate and spatially continuous shallow water bathymetry supports coral reef geomorphological investigation, ecosystem assessment, and marine resource management. However, spectral heterogeneity arising from substrate properties, water depth, and water-column conditions complicates model selection. This study evaluates whether bathymetric model performance differs among observed spectral-reflectance zones and whether zonal model selection improves overall retrieval. ICESat-2 bathymetric points, Sentinel-2 imagery, and Allen Coral Atlas data were analyzed at Lingyang Reef, Huaguang Reef, and East Cay Reef. Representative substrate classes identified using Allen Coral Atlas data were used to derive Sentinel-2 green-band reflectance thresholds. Water pixels were then classified into high-, medium-, and low-reflectance zones. The band-ratio, multiple linear regression (MLR), random forest (RF), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models were constructed and validated within each zone. When averaged across the three study areas, MLR achieved the best performance in the high reflectance zones, with mean R2 and RMSE values of 0.71 and 0.49 m, respectively. RF achieved the best mean performance in the medium reflectance zones, with mean R2 and RMSE values of 0.89 and 0.62 m. In the low reflectance zones, RF and XGBoost outperformed Stumpf and MLR, with XGBoost yielding mean R2 and RMSE values of 0.85 and 1.20 m, respectively. The optimal outputs from the different reflectance zones were integrated and smoothed to generate continuous bathymetric maps. The integrated zonal method achieved RMSE values of 0.76, 0.61, and 0.84 m at the three reefs, respectively, representing numerical reductions of approximately 3.8%, 4.7%, and 12.5% relative to the best unified model. These findings demonstrate that observed spectral-reflectance zoning provides a practical basis for matching bathymetric models to different reflectance conditions, supporting bathymetric mapping in heteroge

extra.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
extra.gist: Satellite bathymetry using ICESat-2 and Sentinel-2 improves mapping of shallow coral reef topography by accounting for spectral heterogeneity. Better reef surveying tools support conservation and ecosystem assessment.

items.title: Inside a German Saltwater LFS! Low-Maintenance Reefing & Simple Coral Care with Mr. Saltwater Tank
items.author: SaltwaterAquarium
items.raw_text: 10-27-2026 Join Mr. Saltwater Tank on location at Korallen Garten Store in Penzberg, Germany, for an exclusive tour with shop owner Brigitte! In this episode, we explore how this second-generation local fish store (LFS) keeps reef keeping simple, low-maintenance, and fun. Brigitte shares her unique approach to saltwater aquariums—from running low-tech soft coral setups without heavy testing to aquascaping with generous live rock for natural fish behavior. We cover the differences between US and European fish stores, freshwater vs. saltwater setups, how to catch elusive tank mates, and timeless advice for beginners setting up their very first marine aquarium. ______________________________________________ ⚠️ Products In This Video ► Real Reef Rock Large 8-16" (by the pound) - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/real-reef-rock-large-8-16-by-the-pound-real-reef/ ► AI Nero 5 Wave Pump (3000 GPH) w/Fish Guard - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/ai-nero-5-wave-pump-3000-gph-w-fish-guard-aquaillumination/ ► Tunze Osmolator 3 Automatic Water Top Off (ATO) 3154 - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/osmolator-3-automatic-water-top-off-ato-3154-tunze/ ► Hanna Instruments HI97115UC Bluetooth Marine Master Multiparameter Checker - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/hi97115uc-bluetooth-marine-master-multiparameter-checker-hanna-instruments/ ► AI Hydra 32 HD Aquarium LED, Black - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/ai-hydra-32-hd-aquarium-led-black-aquaillumination/ ► Kessil A360XE Tuna Blue Saltwater Aquarium LED Light - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/a360xe-tuna-blue-saltwater-aquarium-led-light-kessil/ ► Bubble Magus Curve 5 Elite Protein Skimmer Sicce SK-200 - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/curve-5-elite-protein-skimmer-sicce-sk-200-bubble-magus/ ► Red Sea Reefer RSK-300 Protein Skimmer - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com/reefer-rsk-300-protein-skimmer-red-sea/ ______________________________________________ Website - https://www.saltwateraquarium.com Follow us on Facebook - htt

items.title: Subsidies that fuel overfishing and damage coral reefs and mangroves are costing governments and societies…
items.raw_text: Subsidies that fuel overfishing and damage coral reefs and mangroves are costing governments and societies far more than what is being spent on them, with the total damage across all sectors put at up to $24.7 trillion a year. https://oceanographicmagazine.com/news/subsidies-draining-the-sea-cost-governments-more-than-they-spend/

extra.gist: Fishing subsidies cost governments far more in environmental damage than they spend, harming coral reefs and mangroves. The economics are dense, but the scale of subsidy-driven reef destruction is worth tracking.
